extracted.intended_audience: general readers, aspiring slam poets, slam organizers, and students of contemporary poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative conventions for creating and performing slam poetry at live poetry slam events, including eligibility, performance rules, time limits, allowed/no‑allowed elements, venue norms, and audience‑based judging/scoring procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open eligibility / who may compete
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone, regardless of age, race, sex, education, class, disability, gender, or sexuality, can compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slam poetry is inclusive by design; most venues adhere to an open-entry policy allowing wide community participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship / originality of poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems can be about any subject but typically are supposed to be the creation of the performing poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality/ownership is expected — performers generally present their own work rather than reading others' poems; venues may enforce this as a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter permissiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems can be about any subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no formal content restrictions implied by the guideline; slam often embraces personal, political, and unconventional themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit (3 minutes + grace period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems are not to exceed a 3-minute limit (with 10-second grace period); if they do, points are deducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict timing is enforced in many slams — the typical rule is 3:00 maximum with a 10-second leeway, after which judges deduct points or otherwise penalize the performer.

rubrics_metrics.name: No props
rubrics_metrics.description: No props may be used when performing the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances should rely on voice and body rather than physical stage props; organizers may disallow any external items that alter the performance setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: No musical accompaniment (but vocal/body sounds allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: No musical accompaniment or musical instruments may be used when performing, but the poet is allowed to sing, clap, hum, or make noise with the mouth or other body parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live or recorded instrumental backing is typically prohibited, while performer-generated vocalizations and percussive/body sounds are acceptable as part of the live performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solo or group performance allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may perform on their own or in groups with other poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both solo pieces and ensemble/group pieces are common; teams and group entries are permitted depending on the event's format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry slams are held in any venue that welcomes them, such as parks, bookstores, coffeehouses, and bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers seek accessible public spaces; venue choice can shape audience size, atmosphere, and technical constraints (e.g., sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience power and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience has the power to praise or, sometimes, destroy a poem and from the high-energy performance style of the poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slam places heavy emphasis on audience response and engagement — performers should aim for an energetic delivery and direct connection with listeners, as audience reaction factors into the event's dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging / scoring method (audience judges 0–10; drop highs/lows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets would perform their work and then be judged by five random audience members on a scale of 0 to 10. Out of the five, the highest and lowest scores were dropped and the three remaining scores were added to give the poet an overall score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This common scoring procedure (five random audience judges, 0–10 scale, drop high/low, sum remaining three) produces a single numeric score per performance and determines winners in competitive rounds.
